after.title: Household sharing: invite family, find moved servers and hand a server over
after.map:
## Destination

A family member opens one invitation link, installs the app if needed and joins the household's server. When every saved address of that server stops answering, the app finds its current addresses in the household registry on lar.works and reconnects to the same server identity, without the owner sending a new invitation.

## Decisions

- The registry accepts signed household records only from servers holding a valid server pass; only devices holding the household's share secret can read them.
- Invitation addresses are full URLs with ports, so a changed port is a changed address; overlay ranges and bracketed IPv6 addresses count as private.
- A new device's first sign-in goes through the platform: one browser sheet for Lar sign-in, then a list of the households the person belongs to.
- Every invitation is one lar.works link that carries the whole invitation in the URL fragment, so lar.works never receives it.
- When an owner sets a server up again, the registry keeps the server it replaced and names it, so apps can follow it once and say so.

## Boundaries

- Public server listings, media relay, billing changes and server backups.
- Adding a device while the platform is down on clients other than Apple's.
- Testing on an IPv6-only network.

## Check

Released apps join, recover and sign in against the live platform and a household server.

- A phone on cellular without the app joins through an emailed invitation link.
- After the router's external port changes, a signed-in phone on cellular reconnects by itself within a minute.
- A device with no saved server signs in with Lar and connects at home and on cellular.

items.title: Household sharing: invite family, find moved servers and hand a server over

map.destination: A family member opens one invitation link, installs the app if needed and joins the household's server. When every saved address of that server stops answering, the app finds its current addresses in the household registry on lar.works and reconnects to the same server identity, without the owner sending a new invitation.
decisions: The registry accepts signed household records only from servers holding a valid server pass; only devices holding the household's share secret can read them.
Invitation addresses are full URLs with ports, so a changed port is a changed address; overlay ranges and bracketed IPv6 addresses count as private.
A new device's first sign-in goes through the platform: one browser sheet for Lar sign-in, then a list of the households the person belongs to.
Every invitation is one lar.works link that carries the whole invitation in the URL fragment, so lar.works never receives it.
When an owner sets a server up again, the registry keeps the server it replaced and names it, so apps can follow it once and say so.
Gating settled the details: sessions last 90 days from last use and registry lookups are rate limited per household.
Real-network checks narrowed the address rules: only addresses a device actually reached are marked confirmed.
Apple TV signs in with a code shown on screen; it never opens the browser sheet.
boundaries: Public server listings, media relay, billing changes and server backups.
Adding a device while the platform is down on clients other than Apple's, which iCloud Keychain covers there. It returns with an Android app.
Testing on an IPv6-only network and a registry backup-restore drill.
The App Store release and its Smart App Banner.
